blocks.text: My Sister Stole My Company at Thanksgiving—But She Didn’t Know What Dad Had Already Signed
Not because Fallon had announced she was taking my company.
But because my father, Allaric, suddenly looked as though someone had pulled the floor out from beneath him.
I was fifteen when I started my company.
While other teenagers spent their afternoons hanging out with friends, I sat in our family’s garage, surrounded by cardboard boxes, a secondhand laptop, and handwritten business plans.
My first product was a small collection of handmade home accessories. I sold them online, packed every order myself, and saved almost every dollar I earned.

At eighteen, I rented my first small workspace. At twenty-one, I hired my first employees. By twenty-six, the little business from our garage had become a multimillion-dollar company with offices in three states.
The late nights. The rejected proposals. The customers who trusted me before anyone else did.
And most importantly, I never forgot that nobody in my family believed I could succeed.
She had once slipped me a small envelope containing five hundred dollars and told me something I never forgot.
“Build something nobody can take away from you.”
The announcement nobody expected
Our Thanksgiving dinner was held at my house, a beautiful property overlooking a lake.
I had invited my parents, Fallon, her husband, and several relatives.
Fallon arrived almost an hour late, wearing a designer maternity dress and carrying a champagne bottle.
She was six months pregnant and had recently become unusually interested in my business.
She had asked about our annual revenue, our investors, and even the company’s legal structure.
After dinner, just as the turkey had been carved and the dessert plates were being cleared, Fallon stood up.
“As everyone knows, Dad has always wanted the family business to stay in the family. Well, he’s finally made that happen.”
“Dad transferred Everleigh & Co. to me.”
A few relatives exchanged surprised looks.
“Starting next month, I’ll be taking over as CEO and majority owner. Dad believes it’s time for a fresh perspective.”
“That’s interesting. When exactly did this happen?”
“Well, I didn’t want to spoil Thanksgiving.”
Then came the sentence that made my stomach tighten.
“Besides, you should be grateful Dad gave you the opportunity to build it. You’re getting nothing from the transfer.”
“Don’t make this difficult. Fallon has a baby coming. She needs stability. You’ve already had your success.”
I had spent eleven years building that company.
And apparently, my reward was being told to step aside because my sister needed something.
I reached for my vodka, took one sip, and looked directly at my father.
“Dad, should I tell them now, or do you want to?”
The document that changed everything
Three days earlier, I had received an unusual call from our company’s attorney, Margaret Ellis.
She had been handling our corporate legal affairs for almost eight years.
“Can you come to my office tomorrow morning? There’s something involving your father that you need to see.”
Margaret placed a thick folder on her desk.
Inside were documents showing that my father had attempted to transfer a controlling interest in Everleigh & Co. to Fallon.
He had presented the paperwork as though he had authority to make that decision.
The company had been incorporated in my name when I was eighteen. I had personally retained the controlling voting shares, and every subsequent ownership agreement had been properly documented.
My father had once invested a relatively small amount during our expansion.
That investment had been repaid years earlier.
He had no authority to transfer my shares.
She showed me an email exchange between my father and an outside business consultant.
They had been discussing a proposed acquisition of Everleigh & Co.
The consultant believed Fallon would become the company’s new controlling owner.
My father and sister weren’t simply trying to take my company.
They were preparing to sell something that didn’t belong to them.
“Your father has also been telling potential buyers that you’ve agreed to retire from the business.”
“I know. That’s why I’ve prepared a formal notice confirming the ownership structure and rejecting the unauthorized transfer.”
“No. But we need to address the false representations immediately.”
It was a letter from my grandmother, Eleanor, who had passed away two years earlier.
Margaret explained that Eleanor had requested it be kept with the company’s original ownership records.
The first sentence made my hands go still.
To my granddaughter, the only person in this family who understands what it means to build something from nothing.
And suddenly, I understood why Margaret had asked me to come personally.
My grandmother’s final protection
Years before she passed away, my grandmother had become concerned about my father’s attitude toward the company.
She had watched him dismiss my work, praise Fallon for doing nothing, and repeatedly suggest that family assets should eventually belong to the child he considered more deserving.
